new.title: General-purpose equations of state for hadron-quark matter: first application to accretion-induced phase transitions in neutron stars
new.summary: Strong first-order phase transitions in the cores of neutron stars (NSs) can have profound implications for astrophysical observables, however, their existence remains an open question. Since most NSs form in binary systems, they are expected to experience prolonged episodes of mass accretion that gradually increase their central density and can potentially trigger such a transition. This might, in turn, generate observable multi-messenger signals, as suggested by previous studies. Motivated by this prospect, we generate a new set of equations of state for hadron--quark matter with first-order phase transitions of various strengths, including neutrino absorption opacities in the quark phase as well. We then perform general-relativistic radiation hydrodynamics simulations of NSs undergoing accretion-induced phase transitions. In contrast to previous findings, our results indicate that these systems do not produce unbound ejecta for the models considered, making accretion-induced phase transitions unlikely sources of observable electromagnetic transients. However, we find that transitions are accompanied by intense neutrino emission, with peak luminosities reaching $\sim10^{52}~\mathrm{erg/s}$ for the strongest transition considered. To facilitate future numerical studies, we make the family of equations of state and neutrino opacities used in this work publicly available, enabling the systematic exploration of the role of the phase transition strength.

new.title: The deepest X-ray view of a kiloparsec scale jet at z=6.1
new.summary: The mechanism responsible for the high-energy emission observed in kiloparsec-scale jets across cosmic time remains poorly understood. The relativistic jet associated with the z=6.1 AGN PSO J030947.49+271757.31 is the highest-redshift large-scale jet currently resolved in X-rays, providing a unique opportunity to study these structures. We present new Chandra observations, combined with archival data, for a total exposure of 360 ks. The increased exposure allowed us to resolve the extended X-ray emission into two distinct, slightly resolved components and perform spatially resolved spectral analyses. The extended emission has a photon index of Gamma = 2.25 (+0.45, -0.44), steeper than that of the core (Gamma = 1.86 +/- 0.09), and an extended-to-core luminosity ratio of 18%. Simulations using the Chandra image as input show that an AXIS-like mission could increase the detected photon statistics by a factor of approximately 17. We resolve the kiloparsec-scale jet into two main components and constrain its spectral properties. This is the most distant and one of the most X-ray-luminous large-scale jets currently known. Future X-ray missions with arcsecond-scale angular resolution could enable more detailed studies of such systems and reveal a population of fainter high-redshift jets beyond Chandra's reach.

new.title: Gone Without a Bang: A Search for Failed Core-Collapse Supernovae in ZTF and Predictions for Rubin and Roman
new.summary: The core-collapse of massive stars (${\geq}10\ \rm M_\odot$) usually takes the form of a supernova, but in some cases may lead to a direct collapse, leading to a failed core-collapse supernova (FccSN). Wide-field time-domain surveys, such as the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF), are a useful tool to find such ``disappearing" stars. We use a piecewise linear function model to search the entire ZTF optical photometric catalog for FccSNe, yielding 125 ``faders" that dip significantly with a flat top and bottom flux. Although no candidates were definitively found, some of the sources exhibit promising behavior that may indicate a direct collapse event. Assuming a null result from the search, we calculate at 99\% credibility that the maximum statistical rate of FccSNe in the Milky Way is 147 per century. To contextualize these findings, we also simulate the formation of stellar populations in Milky Way-like galaxies to estimate the expected number of FccSNe observable by ZTF. This simulation predicts ZTF to observe $0.234\pm0.006$ FccSNe per century, which aligns with the lack of definitive observations in ZTF. However, we predict that similar monitoring using the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's Wide Field Instrument (WFI) could enable population-level studies of nearby FccSNe.

new.title: Nuclear Millimeter Continuum Emission in Radio-Quiet Active Galactic Nuclei: an ALMA Spectral and Variability Study
new.summary: Unresolved millimeter (mm) emission is observed in radio-quiet (RQ) Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN), but its physical origin remains debated. Self-absorbed synchrotron emission from the compact X-ray corona is one of the leading candidates. Previous support for this coronal synchrotron origin has mainly been based on variability and spectral indices in a few RQ AGN, with a lack of (quasi-)simultaneous broadband data for larger samples. We present Atacama Large Millimeter/sub-millimeter Array (ALMA) observations of nine nearby ($z \sim 0.008-0.064$) RQ AGN, obtained quasi-simultaneously at 100, 145, and 233 GHz. Based on power-law fits to the spectral energy distributions, we measure millimeter spectral indices ranging from $-0.05^{+0.09}_{-0.09}$ to $0.88^{+0.12}_{-0.11}$. Furthermore, across two 100 GHz observing epochs per source, separated by $4-11$ days, we detect flux density variability of $30-56$% (>$3\sigma$ significance level) in three out of nine sources. Spectral slopes alone are insufficient to constrain the origin of the millimeter emission; however, the observed short-timescale variability and inferred brightness temperature values are consistent with a non-thermal emission mechanism arising from a compact emitting region with a size of $R_{\rm mm}< 10^3 - 10^4 R_{\rm g}$, such as the corona or a compact jet. Furthermore, we find a clear correlation between the 100/233 GHz and X-ray flux in our sample, and establish a new linear correlation between 145 GHz and X-ray emission.

new.title: Chandra and Multiwavelength Study of Pevatron Candiate HESS J1702-420A
new.summary: Aims: HESS J1702-420A is a promising Galactic PeVatron candidate whose physical nature remains unknown. Previous XMM-Newton observations revealed hard, apparently extended X-ray emission from XMMU J170147.3-421407, offset from the center of the TeV source, suggesting a possible pulsar wind nebula (PWN) association. We aim to resolve its X-ray morphology, investigate compact-object candidates in the field, and assess their possible association with HESS J1702-420A. Methods: We obtained three new ACIS-I observations from the Chandra X-ray observatory (CXO) with a total exposure of 50.4 ks. We performed imaging, source detection, spectral and variability analyses, and multiwavelength (MW) machine-learning (ML) source classification. Neutron star (NS) candidates were further investigated using deep near-infrared and radio imaging. Results: The Chandra observations resolve XMMU J170147.3-421407 into a faint point-like source, Src11 (CXO J170144.5-421415), and asymmetric diffuse emission comprising eastern and western lobes. The X-ray spectral, variability, and MW properties of Src11 and the diffuse emission are consistent with those commonly observed in pulsar/PWN systems, further supported by the ML classifications. However, the asymmetric diffuse morphology is unlike a typical bow-shock/tail or jet/torus PWN, and the $\sim7'$ offset from HESS J1702-420A makes a firm physical association difficult to establish. A possible shell-like radio structure north-west of Src11 may indicate a more complex PWN/SNR environment. Other NS candidates are less consistent with a pulsar/PWN interpretation, making Src11 the most compelling candidate in the field.

new.title: Simulations of a Conducting Sphere Moving through Magnetized Plasma II: Effect of Internal Magnetic Fields and Enhancement of Alfvénic Drag
new.summary: Magnetic interaction between astrophysical objects can play an important role and produce electromagnetic radiation in various systems, ranging from planet-moon and star-planet systems to binary compact objects. We extend our previous numerical study of an ideal magnetized plasma flowing past a conducting sphere to the case where the sphere is magnetized. Such a flow generates magnetic disturbances and produces a drag force on the sphere. We examine the drag coefficient as a function of the strength and orientation of the conductor's internal magnetic field relative to the background magnetic field. We find that a strong internal magnetic field that is aligned with the background field significantly enhances the drag coefficient compared to the unmagnetized case; this enhancement is related to the increased magnetic flux that connects the conductor and the open, external field region. We also explore how the drag coefficient changes as the flow transitions from the sub-Alfvénic to the super-Alfvénic regime. Our results suggest that magnetic interaction may play a larger role in orbital evolution of some binary systems than previously expected.

new.title: Multiwavelength Classification of Chandra Sources in Omega Centauri
new.summary: We present a comprehensive study of X-ray sources in the globular cluster NGC 5139 to date. Over 200 Chandra sources are cross-matched to multiwavelength catalogs from HST, JWST, and MeerKAT. We employ a machine-learning classification pipeline (MUWCLASS) for the first time in such a crowded stellar environment and introduce the globular-cluster-specific training dataset, which compiles previously classified sources from 25 Galactic globular clusters. Given the challenges presented by the high-density environment, we compare the MUWCLASS results with traditional classification methods. We confirm counterpart associations suggested in previous works and also identify new confident and candidate associations. We discuss the implications of our classification results in light of models of cluster dynamical evolution and binary formation/destruction.

new.title: Early panchromatic spectra reveal helium in the thermonuclear supernova 2024kce
new.summary: Faint Type I supernovae blur the boundaries between spectroscopic classes, obscuring their progenitors and explosion mechanisms. One proposed origin is a double detonation, in which ignition of an accreted helium shell triggers the explosion of a carbon oxygen white dwarf. Surviving helium is a direct prediction of this mechanism, but its strongest near-infrared feature overlaps with carbon and is ambiguous in isolation. Here we present SN 2024kce, observed with simultaneous optical and near-infrared spectroscopy eleven days before maximum light. We identify He I absorption at three wavelengths, all consistent with a velocity of 16,400 km/s, well above the photosphere. This is the first detection of helium before maximum light in a thermonuclear supernova. Helium at these velocities requires nearby radioactive material for non-thermal excitation, pointing to ash from a detonated surface helium shell. A double detonation model reproduces the optical spectral evolution, suppressed blue flux, and He I 1.083 micron absorption feature. SN 2024kce shares properties with both subluminous Type Ia supernovae and Ia-like calcium-rich transients, providing evidence that the same explosion mechanism operates across these classes. From early optical and near-infrared spectra to Rubin's First Look images, SN 2024kce showcases the full reach of modern observatories in exposing the physics of rare explosions.

new.title: Search for high-energy neutrinos from Einstein Probe detected Fast X-ray Transients using 14 years of IceCube muon track data
new.summary: We perform a time-integrated search for high energy neutrinos from 27 fast X-ray transients (FXTs) detected by Einstein Probe, using 14 years of publicly available IceCube muon-track data. We employ the unbinned maximum likelihood method which is used for IceCube point source searches. We do not find any statistically significant excess from any of the FXTs. The largest TS value is obtained for EP240801a (TS=4.77), corresponding to a local $p$-value of 0.04, which is not significant. We therefore calculate 90\% confidence level upper limit on the differential muon neutrino flux. The most stringent upper limit is obtained for EP241021a, with $E^2 \Phi(E)=2.1\times 10^{-10}$ (GeV cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$), for a $E^{-2}$ spectrum at a pivot energy of 100 TeV.

new.title: Relativistic Dynamical Evolution of Kilonova Spectral Emission
new.summary: We develop a relativistic dynamical model for the thermal evolution of expanding kilonova ejecta, in which the effective temperature is determined by the ejecta mass, opacity, velocity, and radioactive heating rate. The resulting thermal evolution follows a broken power law as the ejecta transition from the optically thick to the optically thin regime. We incorporate this thermal history into a relativistic spectral calculation that accounts for the equal-arrival-time surface geometry and Doppler boosting, enabling us to model the observed kilonova spectrum and constrain the underlying ejecta properties. We investigate the effects of the model parameters and relativistic corrections on the observed temperature and spectral shape, and find that light-travel-time delays and Doppler shifts can produce significant spectral distortions at high ejecta velocities. We apply the model to the early-time X-shooter spectrum of the kilonova AT2017gfo and infer the ejecta mass, opacity, and velocity through Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) fitting with a Student's $t$ likelihood. We find that relativistic effects become increasingly important for fast ejecta ($v \gtrsim 0.5c$), particularly at large viewing angles, where the observed temperature can differ substantially from the rest-frame effective temperature. These results highlight the importance of incorporating relativistic and equal-arrival-time effects when interpreting early-time kilonova spectra, especially for rapidly expanding ejecta.

new.title: Search for Ultra-Relativistic Magnetic Monopoles with LHAASO-KM2A
new.summary: Ultra-relativistic magnetic monopoles traversing the atmosphere are expected to initiate extensive air showers characterized by a muon deficit and a compact lateral profile. Using 1438.81 live days of data from the LHAASO-KM2A array, we present a search for these cosmic particles within the Lorentz factor range of $10^5$ to $10^7$. A machine-learning classifier utilizing lateral shower shape observables from the electromagnetic detectors is deployed to separate the signal from the hadronic background. No statistical excess above the background expectation is observed, and upper limits at the 90\% confidence level are established on the isotropic monopole flux. The resulting upper limit is $2.6 \times 10^{-16}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{sr}^{-1}$ at $\gamma = 10^5$ and reaches $8.8 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{sr}^{-1}$ at $\gamma = 10^7$, which improves upon the astrophysical Parker bound by over three orders of magnitude. This work establishes constraints on the monopole flux within a previously unconstrained velocity window.

new.title: Weak Radio and Bright Early Optical Emission in EP260321a: A Comparative Study with XRO 080109 Reveals the Role of Circumstellar Material Mass
new.summary: Shock breakout (SBO) occurs when a radiation-mediated shock wave, formed during a core-collapse supernova (SN) explosion, breaks out from the stellar surface of the progenitor or from the circumstellar material (CSM), if the CSM is optically thick. The X-ray outburst XRO 080109, associated with a Type Ib/c SN 2008D, has been suggested to be an SBO event from a regular supernova. The recent detection of EP260321a, associated with a broad-lined Type Ic SN 2026gzf, by the Einstein Probe adds a new SBO event. However, the two SBO events differ markedly in their spectra, energetics, late-time radio emission and early optical emission within the first day. We show that the non-detections in radio follow-up observations of EP260321a imply a shock velocity $\lesssim0.1c$, whereas the radio data of XRO 080109 suggest a shock velocity of $\simeq0.2c$. These velocities are consistent with those inferred from the properties of the X-ray outbursts and explain the difference in their X-ray spectra. The X-ray energy and duration of EP260321a indicate that the shock breaks out from the CSM at a radius of $\sim2\times10^{13}\ {\rm cm}$. Its bright optical emission at $t\lesssim1\ {\rm d}$ can be explained by cooling emission from a dense, extended CSM shell heated by the radiation-mediated shock, requiring a total CSM mass of $\sim0.06M_\odot$, substantially larger than that inferred for XRO 080109. Finally, the lower shock velocity and larger CSM mass can be unified in a picture in which a more massive CSM decelerates the radiation-mediated shock more significantly before it breaks out.

new.title: The XMM-Newton view of the DEM L36 superbubble in the Large Magellanic Cloud
new.summary: We present the first multi-wavelength analysis of the DEM L36 superbubble in the Large Magellanic Cloud. We compare the DEM L36 superbubble with other Galactic and Magellanic Cloud superbubbles. We use data from XMM-Newton, supplemented by data from the Magellanic Cloud Emission Line Survey, the Dark Energy Camera Magellanic Cloud Emission Line Survey, the Spitzer Space Telescope, and the Australia Telescope Compact Array. We perform a multi-wavelength morphological analysis to understand the shape and structure of the superbubble and X-ray spectral analysis to derive physical parameters of the hot gas. We find significant X-ray emission in DEM L36, dominated by a central bubble region mostly confined by a thin H$\alpha$ filamentary shell. This has two distinct blowout regions to the east and west, with a possible smaller blowout in the south. Spectral analysis shows the X-ray emission is well fit with a thermal plasma model in collisional ionisation equilibrium with a temperature of $kT=0.17~(0.16-0.18)$ keV and unabsorbed luminosity $L_{X~(0.5-7.0~\mathrm{keV})}=3.62\times 10^{35} $erg s$^{-1}$. Unlike other LMC superbubbles, we find no clear powering cluster at the centre, though relatively small clusters near the edge are likely supplying the mechanical input at the present epoch. We use photometric data of these clusters to estimate cluster masses, ages, and mechanical inputs to compare with the energy stored in the superbubble. We find that these clusters have supplied more energy over their lifetime than is currently observed in the superbubble, indicative of the so-called growth rate discrepancy problem. It is likely the DEM L36 superbubble was initially shaped by a central massive stellar population that has since dispersed and largely lost to supernovae, with smaller clusters at the edges of the swept-up shell being currently supplying the energy input.

new.title: In Search of the Gravitational Wave of Fast X-Ray Transient in the Second Part of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Fourth Observing Run
new.summary: Fast X-ray Transients (FXTs) are brief, intense X-ray flashes unassociated with persistent X-ray sources or known stellar objects, typically lasting from seconds to hours. With the launch of the Einstein Probe in January 2024, the study of FXTs has entered a new phase. Its large field of view significantly increases the discovery rate, enabling more robust statistics. The leading discoveries have revealed a fraction of gamma-ray bursts, while the rest remain unexplained. We propose a methodology to search for possible relations between gravitational waves (GWs) and FXTs, as it may serve as a discrepancy among proposed theoretical models. To achieve this, we intend to utilize X-Pipeline, an unmodeled search algorithm, to identify excess coherent signals in LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) O4b observations. Out of 64 FXTs events, we obtained 19 FXTs for constructing robust searches. Given the absence of any detectable GW signals, we subsequently calculated upper limits and estimated exclusion distances for each source. In order to enrich the sample base and statistical analysis, this methodology could henceforth be conducted through future GW searches, including KAGRA in the O4c and O5 observations.

new.title: Breaking the symmetry: X-ray polarization from a spreading layer on a tilted weakly magnetized neutron star
new.summary: When modeling the emission from an X-ray binary system, we often assume that the rotational axis of the compact object is aligned with that of the binary system. While often considered irrelevant for spectroscopic observations, the orientation of the binary system is crucial for polarimetric properties. With the recent advent of X-ray polarimetric observations enabled by the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE), indications of a possible misalignment of the neutron star rotational axis with respect to the binary axis have been reported. Following these indications, we present an analytical model for the polarimetric properties of emission arising from a spreading layer on an inclined weakly magnetized neutron star (WMNS). We discuss the expected polarimetric properties and study the impact of geometrical parameters of the system on the polarization of WMNS emission. We compare our results with those for aligned systems. Finally, we discuss applications of the model to recent and upcoming X-ray polarimetric observations with IXPE and mention the suggestions for further development of the model.

new.title: Multigroup Radiation Diffusion with Compton Scattering on a Moving Mesh: Implementation in RICH and Application to Tidal Disruption Events
new.summary: Compton scattering exchanges energy between radiation and hot gas and changes the spectrum in high-energy astrophysical systems such as tidal disruption events (TDEs). Because it couples all photon energies and can act faster than the hydrodynamic time step, many radiation-hydrodynamics (RHD) simulations omit its spectral redistribution or treat its energy exchange in the gray approximation. We extend the multigroup flux-limited diffusion module of the moving-mesh RHD code RICH to include Compton scattering with the exact thermal Compton kernel. In our semi-implicit scheme for the thermal radiative transfer equation, the temperature dependence of the kernel enters a generalized Fleck factor, and the group Compton operator conserves photon number and satisfies detailed balance. In equilibration tests, the scheme agrees with independent solutions, relaxes without absorption and emission to a Bose-Einstein spectrum, and remains stable for time steps that do not resolve the Compton equilibration timescale. We apply it to a three-dimensional simulation of the disruption of a $0.5\,M_\odot$ star by a $10^6\,M_\odot$ black hole. We find that during the X-ray flash, inverse Compton scattering dominates the coupling between the gas and the radiation near the nozzle shock, where it adds X-ray energy much faster than thermal emission and may affect the dynamics. Outside the X-ray thermalization radii, its instantaneous X-ray production rate during the flash is comparable to or larger than the escaping X-ray luminosity, so it may contribute substantially to the X-ray emission from TDEs.

new.title: Spectral Properties of X-Ray Flares in Gamma-Ray Bursts
new.summary: We conducted a systematic spectral analysis of the X-ray flares of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) observed by Swift/X-ray Telescope from 2005 April to 2015 March. The sample includes 521 flares from 206 GRBs. The GRBs cover the three subtypes: X-ray flashes (XRFs), X-ray-rich GRBs (XRRs), and classical GRBs (C-GRBs). We used a simple power-law model to fit the spectra during the flares, as well as to fit the preflare and postflare afterglow emissions, and obtained the parameters such as photon index and intrinsic hydrogen column density ($N_{\rm H}$). By comparing the spectral characteristics of flares, prompt emission, and afterglow emission, and analyzing the temporal evolution of the X-ray flare spectra, we obtained the following main conclusions. (1) The spectrum during the flare phase is significantly harder than that of the preflare and postflare phases, while there is no obvious difference in the spectrum between the preflare and postflare phases. (2) The intrinsic $N_{\rm H}$ shows no significant change between the preflare and flare phases, but significantly decreases after the flare. (3) The overall X-ray flare spectra are softer than those of the prompt emission. (4) For GRBs with multiple flares, the photon index softens with increasing flare peak time. (5) The X-ray flare spectra in XRFs are softer than those in C-GRBs. These results support the origin of X-ray flares being from the internal shock radiation driven by the late activity of the GRB central engine.

new.title: FRB 20210601A: Extreme Temporal Clustering in a Repeating Fast Radio Burst Source as Evidence for a Hidden Class of Episodic Repeaters
new.summary: Population studies of fast radio burst (FRB) repetition typically model sources using a single distribution of steady, time-averaged burst rates, yet individual sources show significant departures from this assumption. Here we present FRB 20210601A, a source discovered by the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment FRB project (CHIME/FRB) that represents the most extreme such departure yet identified. The source produced at least nine bursts within a single 106.5 s interval -- the highest instantaneous burst rate yet reported from a repeating FRB source at $\gtrsim 2$ Jy ms fluences -- yet remained otherwise undetected despite $\sim 320$ hr of exposure spanning 7 yr. The active interval occurred while the source was in a side-lobe of the CHIME/FRB digitized beams, implying an instantaneous burst rate $\gtrsim2.3\times$ higher ($\gtrsim$ 21 bursts) at main-lobe sensitivity. The source's intense, brief burst storm flanked by apparent quiescence despite substantial exposure is unique among the CHIME/FRB repeater sample, although its burst morphology, excess dispersion measure ($\rm{DM_{excess}} \sim 360$ pc cm$^{-3}$), Faraday rotation measure ($|\rm{RM_{excess}}| \sim 150-170$ rad m$^{-2}$), and temporal scattering ($\tau \lesssim 0.37$ ms at 600 MHz) are otherwise typical. Modeling a population of episodically active repeaters (i.e., short burst storms separated by long recurrence times) and accounting for declination-dependent exposure, we forecast $\sim1-4$ additional source discoveries similar to FRB 20210601A over the next decade of CHIME/FRB operations, corresponding to a CHIME/FRB-detectable population of $9^{+200}_{-8}$ sources (68% credible interval). These results demonstrate that highly episodic repeaters could constitute a selection-biased but detectable component of the FRB population, possibly reflecting distinct magnetospheric states or triggering mechanisms.

new.title: Prompt Jet Launching and Delayed Thermal Disk in Tidal Disruption Event for Prolonged Activity GRB 220706A
new.summary: GRB 220706A exhibits X-ray flaring activity extending to ~51 days after the trigger, along with a luminous optical thermal component emerging on a timescale of ~10^6 s. Such prolonged central-engine activity could be powered by a collapsar fed by an extended stellar envelope. However, a relativistic jet may struggle to break out of the extended envelope. These challenges motivate a tidal disruption event (TDE), although explaining both the early relativistic jet and the luminous late optical thermal emission within one TDE framework remains difficult. We investigate a TDE scenario in which shocks between stellar debris streams drive the early inflow of some debris, potentially carrying preexisting fossil magnetic flux toward the black hole (BH) and powering an initial relativistic jet via the Blandford-Znajek mechanism. The remaining debris circularizes into an accretion disk, whose thermal emission accounts for the late optical thermal component. For GRB 220706A, the optical timescale, luminosity, and color temperature are consistent with disruption of a blue supergiant (M_*~50M_{sun}, R_*~20~R_{sun}) by a BH of mass M_{BH}~10^5 M_{sun}, assuming that the accretion disk forms on a timescale comparable to the orbital period of the most tightly bound stellar debris. A magnetic field strength of ~10^5 G is required near the BH before disruption to power a jet capable of producing the inferred gamma-ray luminosity. Continued fallback may sustain central-engine activity beyond the observed X-ray flaring episode, making future X-ray monitoring a test of this scenario.

new.title: Charged fluid tori with an approximate magnetic self-field around magnetized Schwarzschild black holes: A semi-analytic approach
new.summary: We study toroidal structures formed by a charged, non-self-gravitating perfect fluid orbiting a Schwarzschild black hole immersed in a poloidal magnetic field. To obtain analytic and semi-analytic solutions, we assume a cold, rest-mass-dominated fluid with uniform specific charge and zero conductivity, so the current is purely convective. This regime is formally opposite to the ideal GRMHD limit. The total magnetic field comprises a prescribed asymptotically uniform external component and an approximate self-field associated with the azimuthal current in the torus. We represent the latter by a regularized dipole approximation to the field of an effective circular current loop. Neglecting the self-field, the method of characteristics yields a general implicit solution of the integrability condition for a function parametrizing the specific-angular-momentum profile. A separately obtained cylindrically dependent class recovers a solution from our earlier work. For the radially dependent class, we integrate the Euler equations, obtain the enthalpy potential, and derive local conditions for equatorially centered tori. We then examine the field-free limit, both magnetic components separately, and their superposition. The external field supports closed tori within analytically derived parameter bounds, whereas no such equilibrium is found for the isolated approximate self-field within the numerically explored domain. In a representative combined-field sequence, the radial extent varies nonmonotonically with relative self-field strength: it increases for weak self-fields and decreases as the self-field becomes comparable to the external field. The results show how an approximate magnetic self-field modifies the morphology and domain of existence of charged-fluid tori.

new.title: Formation and Detectability of PSR J0653+0443-like Extremely Eccentric Binary Neutron Stars in the Milky Way
new.summary: Recently, the Five-hundred-meter-Aperture-Spherical-radio-Telescope (FAST) Galactic Plane Pulsar Snapshot (GPPS) survey discovers an extraordinary binary neutron star (BNS) system, PSR J0653+0443, possessing the highest known orbital eccentricity ($e\approx0.992$) among Galactic BNSs (Yang et al., 2026), which provides a unique probe into the formation and evolution of BNSs. In this Letter, we perform compact binary population synthesis calculations with self-consistent neutron star spin evolution to model extremely eccentric BNS population detectable by the FAST GPPS survey, explicitly incorporating observational selection effects. We find that BNSs with $e>0.99$ constitute only $\sim0.6\%$ of the detectable population, with an expected detection number of $\lambda_{\mathrm{GPPS}}\approx0.31$ over the full planned footprint. Thus, although rare, systems as eccentric as PSR J0653+0443 are compatible with standard binary evolution. We further demonstrate that extremely eccentric BNSs arise preferentially from core-collapse supernovae, whereas imposing $P\lesssim0.1$ s select older, more frequently recycled systems, which naturally reproduce the observed properties of PSR J0653+0443. We further predict that the completed GPPS sample has a $\sim15\%$ chance of finding another $e>0.99$ BNS, but a much higher $\sim88\%$ chance for $e>0.90$ systems. By contrast, future facilities are expected to enlarge the detectable highly eccentric BNS population, with SKA potentially detecting PSR J0653+0443-like systems and sub-mHz gravitational-wave detectors probing a larger population with $e>0.9$, enabling much more in-depth population-level constraints.

cross.title: Confirming candidate self-lensing binary detections with radial velocity measurements
cross.summary: Compact objects in approximately edge-on binary orbits with stars are able to produce a self-lensing effect, amplifying light from their companion once per orbit. To date, five white dwarf self-lensing systems are known, while none are known containing black holes or neutron stars. Discovery of such systems is a potential method of finding quiescent black holes and neutron stars, most of which will be pristine and unchanged from their formation. Photometric detections can suffer from degeneracies in the lens mass and orbital parameters when the amplification and crossing time are not well constrained, while photometric searches produce too many false positives to allow radial velocity investigation of every candidate. Therefore we investigate the minimal radial velocity (RV) observational requirements to characterise such systems by simulating detectable self-lensing light curves, using those light curves to generate targeted RV observations, and fitting RV jointly with photometry. We evaluate the median relative error in the recovered lens mass and orbital period, alongside compact-object class recovery. We find that adding RV measurements substantially reduces parameter error, with compact-object class generally easier to determine than the exact lens mass. Parameter accuracy is driven mainly by number of RV observations, with RV precision playing a weaker role except for the shortest-period systems, with even a small number of RV measurements resulting in substantial improvement in accuracy. These results suggest that multi-stage RV follow-up, starting with a small number of observations of many candidates, can efficiently classify self-lensing candidates and identify high-priority systems for further investigation.

cross.title: $γ$hosts from the past: reheating neutron stars with supernova-sourced ALPs
cross.summary: Axion-like particles (ALPs) can be copiously produced in the hot and dense environment of a core-collapse supernova. If their mass is within an order of magnitude of the supernova temperature, a non-negligible fraction of them will remain gravitationally bound to the neutron star remnant. This basin of ALPs can then decay to photons over the lifetime of the neutron star, thereby reheating it. Using the measured luminosities of several neutron stars, we close multiple windows in ALP parameter space while also satisfying the SN 1987A cooling constraint on the ALP-nucleon coupling. In particular, using the 35000 K upper limit on the temperature of the coldest neutron star observed, PSR J2144$-$3933, we derive the strongest upper limits on the ALP-photon coupling for 1$-$400 MeV ALP masses. Ceilings on these limits arising from ALP decays occurring within the neutron star lifetime may be overcome by using younger neutron stars such as the one in Cas A, probing couplings orders of magnitude higher. Observations of a $2000 \, {\rm K}$-hot neutron star in infrared observatories such as the James Webb Space Telescope could reach ALP-photon couplings three orders lower and ALP masses one order lower than our current limits.

cross.title: Variable-phase methods and data for long-range scattering
cross.summary: Long-range interactions play an important role in dark-matter phenomenology, affecting the relic abundance, indirect-detection signals, and structure formation on galactic scales. Reliable predictions often require nonperturbative solutions of the Schrödinger equation over broad parameter ranges and many partial waves. We present a numerical framework based on the variable-phase method, which recasts the radial Schrödinger equation as a system of first-order equations and allows both regular and irregular solutions to be computed efficiently. The former determine phase shifts and Sommerfeld factors, while the latter provide additional information relevant for the self-consistent unitarization of contact-like inelastic interactions. We discuss the numerical implementation, integration-domain selection, partial-wave convergence, and comparisons with analytic limits. We release the code together with tables for the Yukawa potential containing phase shifts, Sommerfeld factors, elastic and angularly weighted cross sections, and the irregular-solution information relevant for unitarization. These resources facilitate dark-matter studies without requiring repeated computationally intensive scans.

cross.title: Charting the Galactic Underworld II: Strategies for Identifying BHs and NSs with LISA
cross.summary: Stellar-mass black holes (BHs) and neutron stars (NSs) observed by space-based gravitational-wave detectors offer constraints on binary stellar evolution that are complementary to those from ground- based detectors. The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) is expected to detect hundreds of double compact objects (DCOs) containing a BH or NS, but distinguishing these sources from the far more numerous double white dwarfs (WDWDs) may prove challenging. We use adaptive importance sampling with COSMIC to synthesise large populations of BHBH, BHNS, NSNS, BHWD, and NSWD binaries. We combine these binaries with a Milky Way star-formation history and integrate their Galactic orbits with cogsworth, repeating our simulations for a grid of variations in uncertain (binary) stellar physics. We find that LISA detections are largely insensitive to the changes in Galactic position resulting from natal kicks. We then assess how well chirp mass, eccentricity, distance from the Galactic plane, and orbital frequency distinguish BH- and NS-hosting DCOs from WDWDs, accounting for LISA measurement uncertainties. Using chirp mass alone distinguishes only 50-60% of BHBHs and BHNSs, and ~40% of NSNSs, but combining this with orbital frequency recovers 90-100% of BHBHs and BHNSs and around ~50% of NSNSs, with eccentricity further improving the recovery of NSNSs to around 60-70%. Distance from the Galactic plane adds little discriminating power, though it can recover a handful of NSWDs that are missed otherwise. These methods will help identify a significantly larger number of BHs and NSs in LISA data that would be missed by a chirp mass cut alone.

cross.title: The black hole-galaxy correlations of the 12 micron local AGN sample: a NuSTAR perspective
cross.summary: The M-sigma correlation of inactive galaxies plays a crucial role in estimating the black hole mass (MBH) in active galactic nuclei (AGN): 1) it is used to calibrate the reverberation mapping (RM) method; 2) the RM is the basis of the single epoch method, the most-used technique to determine MBH of broad-line AGN; and 3) in narrow-line AGN, MBH is often directly inferred from the M-sigma correlation. The main goal of this work is to test whether the M-sigma relation calibrated from inactive galaxies can be reliably applied to a local AGN population spanning Seyfert 1, Seyfert 2, and hidden broad-line region galaxies (HBLRs), and whether the resulting AGN relation has sufficient predictive power to be used as an indirect MBH estimator. To investigate this hypothesis, we used the 12 micron AGN sample, a local representative and largely unbiased sample. Since a substantial fraction of this sample has good-quality NuSTAR data, we estimated their MBH with the X-ray scaling method, which works for any AGN accreting at moderate or high level. We find that the M-sigma correlation of the 12 micron AGN sample is different from the one obtained with inactive galaxies and has a substantial scatter. Therefore, its predictive power for MBH estimates is fairly limited. We also find that the MBH-Mgal correlation based on the 12 micron AGN sample is consistent with the analogous correlation obtained from a large sample of nearby type 1 AGN and inconsistent with that of inactive galaxies. Finally, we find suggestive evidence that Seyfert 1 and HBLRs have similar and systematically higher Eddington ratios than Seyfert 2 galaxies.

cross.title: Evolution of Jeans instability in nonthermal magnetized complex plasmas
cross.summary: The classical Jeans instability framework provides a conceptual foundation for understanding self-gravitational collapse and subsequent star formation in interstellar environments. However, cosmic plasmas are inherently magnetized and frequently collisionless, exhibiting significant departures from local thermodynamic equilibrium. While linear theories predict initial instability thresholds, they fail to track the long-term nonlinear runaway dynamics. We present a fluid simulation investigating the nonlinear evolution of the Jeans instability in a magnetized tricomponent complex (dusty) plasma. The constituent nonthermal electrons and ions are governed by the $\kappa$-distribution law, while the heavier dust grains are treated in a fluid framework, coupled with a uniform ambient magnetic field. The numerical architecture utilizes a fourth-order finite difference method (FDM) for spatial gradients and a second-order leap-frog time-integration scheme. We systematically investigate the complex interplay among the self-gravitational attraction, nonthermal electrostatic screening, and magnetic pressure across a wide range of magnetic field strengths and degrees of nonthermality. It is found that enhanced nonthermality accelerates structural localization, while the magnetic field introduces a critical pressure barrier that suppresses the instability. In highly magnetized environments, thermal and nonthermal systems exhibit identical growth rate characteristics, indicating that magnetic pressure dominates the nonthermal thermostatistics in the strong magnetic regime. This study develops a comprehensive and numerically robust framework to understand early-stage star formation and evolution processes in nonthermal astrophysical media.

cross.title: Same Events, Weaker Bound: Model Dependence in Magellanic Microlensing Limits on Primordial Black Holes
cross.summary: OGLE microlensing of the Magellanic Clouds sets the leading bounds on primordial black holes (PBHs) as dark matter from $10^{-8}$ to $10^{3}\,M_\odot$. Holding the detected events and survey efficiencies fixed, we show that changes to the Milky Way halo, the stellar lens populations and the Large Magellanic Cloud halo, each motivated by recent data, weaken the published strict 20-year bound by up to $\simeq6$, and by over an order of magnitude in an extreme stress test. With primordial clustering, the planetary-mass bound weakens by a factor $3.4$--$6$. We strongly recommend that compact-object dark matter limits be quoted together with their modeling assumptions and, generally, be derived under conservative assumptions.

cross.title: Axial Perturbations of Extended Tolman III in the New $f(R,T)$ Theory
cross.summary: We investigate compact objects using the extended Tolman III equation of state in the framework of $f(R,T)=R+2\chi T$ gravity. In the matter sector of the Lagrangian density, we employ a new formalism based on the evaluation of the second-order derivative of the matter Lagrangian with respect to the metric \cite{Jayawiguna:2026das}. We analyze the corresponding observational signatures through axial gravitational perturbations including stellar stability and gravitational echo. We find that the effective potential in $f(R,T)$ gravity is wider and deeper than its counterpart in general relativity (GR). The quasinormal-mode (QNM) frequencies are calculated using the Bohr--Sommerfeld (BS) fitting and both the lower- and higher-order Wentzel--Kramers--Brillouin (WKB) approximations. For the ultracompact configurations considered, trapped modes can tunnel through the potential barrier, giving rise to gravitational-wave echoes. The imaginary parts of the QNM frequencies are found to be negative, $\Im(\omega_n M)<0$, indicating that the perturbations decay exponentially with time. Our results show that the echo train in GR contains more echoes than that in $f(R,T)$ gravity. Finally, assuming that the stellar object is a neutron star and adopting a stellar radius consistent with measurements by the Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer (NICER), we find that the $f(R,T)$ gravity model yields a characteristic frequency consistent with the estimated frequency associated with GW170817 for $\beta= 4.663\times10^{-1}$ and $\chi=0.96\pi$, whereas the corresponding GR model does not exhibit comparable agreement.

cross.title: Lomb-Scargle Recovery of Periodic Binary Signals across Black Hole Mass and Cadence
cross.summary: Searches for periodic supermassive black hole binaries in quasar light curves rely on recovery fractions, the share of injected signals detected, which forecasts use as detection efficiencies. Lin, Charisi, & Haiman (2026) measured them for the Lomb-Scargle periodogram on damped-random-walk light curves matched to 12,400 bright, high-mass Palomar Transient Factory (PTF) quasars with Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 7 (DR7) masses. To test them over four decades of mass, we inject their sinusoidal and sawtooth signals into light curves of mergers in the TNG100-1 cosmological simulation, with magnitudes drawn from DR7 quasars of similar mass (extrapolated at low mass). We apply their threshold in each frequency bin, set by $10^5$ noise-only light curves per binary, on observed PTF cadences, one Stripe 82 cadence and an LSST-like cadence (Legacy Survey of Space and Time). At fixed absolute magnitude $M_i=-23$, sinusoid recovery falls toward high mass, and with DR7 magnitudes it climbs above about $10^8\,M_\odot$, so the magnitude assignment sets the sign of the trend. Above $10^8\,M_\odot$, where their sample lies, PTF sinusoid recovery is 39.8 against their 44.7 per cent. At LSST-like cadence sinusoid recovery is 76.9 per cent, about three times their 22.6 per cent, for reasons mostly unidentified. Denser sampling of the same PTF baselines did not lower recovery in any test. Even at LSST-like cadence we miss most sawtooth signals above $10^8\,M_\odot$. We tabulate recovery per 0.5-dex mass bin and cadence, with low-mass values likely too high for a deeper survey.

cross.title: EP J062132.0+623837: A Multi-wavelength Study of a Changing-look Active Galactic Nucleus Discovered by Einstein Probe
cross.summary: EP J062132.0+623837 is a new X-ray source identified in 14-day binned survey data from the Wide-field X-ray Telescope aboard the Einstein Probe (EP). Subsequent X-ray observations with the Follow-up X-ray Telescope (FXT) on board EP localized the source to the central region of the galaxy 2MASX J06213207+6238390 at $z=0.084$. Here, we present a comprehensive analysis of the multi-wavelength data for this object. During the FXT and Swift/XRT follow-up, the source remained X-ray active, with observed luminosities of $(3-9)\times10^{43}$ erg s$^{-1}$, and its X-ray spectra were well described by power-law models with photon indices of $\Gamma\sim1.5$. The optical spectrum of the host galaxy clearly reveals a broad-line active galactic nucleus (AGN) exhibiting significantly enhanced broad Balmer emission lines compared to an archival spectrum obtained four years earlier, thereby marking a changing-look transition from Type 1.8 to Type 1.5. Furthermore, long-term optical and mid-infrared light curves indicate that the nucleus underwent dramatic brightening around 2010 and has since shown substantial variability. Given the spatial coincidence and multi-wavelength behavior, we identify EP J062132.0+623837 as a changing-look AGN, initially detected by EP and subsequently confirmed to exhibit large-amplitude variability across multiple bands. This case study demonstrates the great potential of wide-field time-domain X-ray surveys for discovering changing-look AGNs, paving a new avenue for their systematic identification as a powerful complement to ongoing optical surveys.

cross.title: Parameter Constraints on $f(R^{1+ε},T_{μν}T^{μν})$ Gravity from Exotic Compact Objects
cross.summary: According to General Relativity (GR), gravity is described as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. Although GR has been highly successful in describing gravitational phenomena, exotic compact objects with high mass and strong gravitational fields, as well as low-mass objects, have motivated the study of modified theories of gravity. One of the modified gravity frameworks is $f(R,T^2) = R^{1 + \epsilon} + \alpha \kappa^2 T_{\mu \nu} T^{\mu \nu}$, which provides an extension of GR by introducing modifications to both the geometric and matter sectors. In this study, we investigate the mass-radius structure, physical viability, and stability of quark stars in $f(R,T^2)$ gravity using the MIT Bag Model equation of state. We compare results from the exact $f(R,T^2)$ model, its first-order Taylor expansion, and GR. The values of the gravity parameter $\epsilon$ and $\alpha$ are constrained by evaluating the ability of the model to reproduce the observed mass-radius configurations of compact objects, including HESS J1731-347 with a mass of $M = 0.77_{-0.17}^{+0.20} \, M_{\odot}$ and a radius of $R = 10.4_{-0.78}^{+0.86}$ km, GW190814 with a mass of $M = 2.6 \, M_{\odot}$, PSR J1614-2230, with a mass of $M = 1.928 \pm 0.017 \, M_{\odot}$ and a radius of $R > 10$ km, and PSR J0437-4715, with a mass of $M = 1.418 \pm 0.037 \, M_{\odot}$ and a radius of $R = 11.36_{-0.63}^{+0.95}$ km. We assess the physical viability and stability of the stellar configurations using the energy conditions (strong, weak, null, and dominant) and the speed of sound. Overall, the $f(R,T^2)$ gravity model can accommodate quark star configurations and reproduce the observed properties of massive compact objects, particularly those associated with GW190814 and the lightest compact object observed, HESS J1731-347, respectively.

cross.title: Synthetic 2D magnetic turbulence with controlled island structuring
cross.summary: Magnetic turbulence remains up to this day not fully understood, despite its important role in the behavior of plasmas. A recurring ingredient in plasma turbulence is the spontaneous formation and evolution of plasmoids. These represent magnetic islands on current sheets in two-dimensional turbulent magnetic fields that are consistently found in high-resolution direct numerical simulations (DNSs) using a magnetohydrodynamic description. However, such simulations require considerable amounts of computational power. Synthetic turbulence models provide an alternative, cheap approach to the generation of fully-developed turbulent fields. In this work, we first present an extension of our open-source, general synthetic turbulence BxC toolkit that is specifically tailored to generate 2D turbulent magnetic fields. We then use a novel physically motivated, but purely geometric construction that generates current sheet island chains, which results in fields that visually match the ones obtained through DNSs. We show how this construction affects the magnetic field lines and find a correlation with the formation of magnetic O-points and X-points. The magnetic flux and size of the islands in the field are found to match well with theoretical scaling laws. Lastly, we show BxC's capabilities by generating a 2D $N\times N$ turbulent magnetic field of resolution $N = 100000$, going beyond the state-of-the-art reached by simulations, on a single CPU with modest computational resources. Our construction maintains direct control over the inertial range, and allows to make morphological changes to the plasmoids and fields, demonstrating plasmoid appearance, disappearance and merging.

cross.title: Gravitational Wave Diffractive Images Reveal the Structure of Astrophysical Objects
cross.summary: Scattering patterns encode the structure of extended objects, as demonstrated by charged particle scattering on atomic nuclei. Gravitational wave (GW) diffraction offers an analogous probe of otherwise invisible mass distributions. At linear order in the lens potential we derive expressions relating the central diffractive image contribution to a gravitationally lensed GW waveform to the Fourier transform of the projected lens density. For finite mass lenses this contribution takes the form of a point mass Born amplitude multiplied by a normalized mass form factor, analogous to that in nuclear scattering. As the frequency of GWs from a merging compact binary source evolves the signal samples this form factor across spatial scales, imprinting lens structure through interference with the primary image. Using full numerical wave optics calculations we quantify the observational reach for extended dark matter objects, primordial black holes halo-dressed by dark matter halos and superradiance clouds of ultralight bosons around black holes. For the considered source populations, five year observations with next generation detectors can distinguish extended lenses from point masses, probing dark matter fractions down to $\mathcal{O}(10^{-5})$, and halo-dressed primordial black holes from matched bare black holes, probing primordial black hole dark matter fractions down to $\mathcal{O}(10^{-6})$. For sufficiently close source-lens configurations, scalar superradiance clouds can produce distinguishable diffraction signatures for boson masses of approximately $10^{-17}-10^{-12}~\mathrm{eV}$. These results provide a framework for characterizing extended dark matter and compact object astrophysical environments.

cross.title: Simulation-based inference of profile evolution for high-precision pulsar timing
cross.summary: Pulsars are exceptional cosmic laboratories, the most stable of which rival atomic clocks. Nearly all of that precision rests on one observable, the average pulse profile unique to each pulsar and stable over decades. These profiles change shape systematically with observing frequency, reflecting the physics of the emitting pulsar beam, but if left unmodelled, it can bias the arrival-time measurements, undermining precision timing. Profile-domain timing has been proposed to address this effect, but current implementations use stochastic sampling, which is computationally prohibitive and has limited the application in large-scale analyses. Here, we present a simulation-based inference approach to profile-domain timing, using a normalising flow conditioned on a convolutional embedding of the frequency-phase portrait. From a single portrait, it returns joint posteriors on dispersion measures, arrival times, and the parameters governing profile evolution instantaneously, with uncertainties verified against known inputs following an initial training run. The value of a likelihood-free approach is that the simulator becomes the interface to pulsar properties. Fundamental properties like non-Gaussian noise, pulsar self-noise, jitter, scattering, and profile change can be inferred by simulating them rather than by deriving a new likelihood for each, opening a promising pathway to include machine learning methods into pulsar timing workflows.

cross.title: A Generalized Framework for Rapid Polarization Response Generation in Wide Field-of-View Compton Polarimeters
cross.summary: Polarimetry is the most direct probe of the unsettled radiation mechanism and magnetic field structure of gamma-ray burst (GRB) prompt emission at the energies where it peaks, tens of keV to about 1 MeV. Compton polarimeters use the azimuthal scattering angle distribution (ASAD), a 180 degree modulation on axis. GRB measurements have largely relied on the on-axis modulation factor $\mu_{100}$. For a wide field-of-view planar polarimeter, GRBs arrive off axis, where the Klein-Nishina projection adds harmonics to the ASAD. Muleri (2014) described this projection and evaluated it in a low-energy expansion for X-rays. We evaluate it numerically without approximation over the whole prompt-emission energy band for any incidence and polarization angles, quantify the off-axis harmonics a single modulation factor cannot capture, and verify the model against GEANT4 simulations of an ideal polarimeter. We also include the effect of the detection threshold on the ASAD. With POLAR as the case study, we present two modes that build the full polarization response with at least 95 percent fewer Monte Carlo simulations. Mode 1 takes only the unpolarized simulation per energy and recovers the polarization measured with POLAR's full GEANT4 responses for all but the brightest GRBs, where it underestimates the polarization degree. Mode 2 adds two polarized simulations per energy at distinct angles and reproduces the simulated ASADs to their statistical noise and the polarization of every GRB tested. Both modes are released as open-source software for any planar Compton polarimeter.

cross.title: Boosted Dark Matter Directionality in Large Liquid Scintillator Detectors
cross.summary: Light dark matter can be boosted by cosmic-ray-dark matter interactions, which opens the possibility of direct-detection searches with large neutrino detectors. We consider the signal produced by boosted dark matter undergoing quasi-elastic scattering off carbon and knocking out a neutron in a large liquid scintillator detector. A distinctive delayed gamma ray from neutron capture can be reconstructed after $\sim 210$ $\mu$s, which is paired up with the prompt signal during neutron propagation. We find that 100 kt$\cdot$yr of data from the neutron-coincidence channel will be able to probe new parameter space compared to free proton signals found in previous work. We further consider the possibility of utilizing directional information from the displaced vertex associated with the capture of the final-state neutron. However, we find that directional information does not materially improve the sensitivity due to the large nucleon scattering angle.

repl.title: Identifying galactic binary systems of neutron stars and black holes with LISA
repl.summary: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect $\sim 100$ galactic binary systems comprised of black holes and neutron stars. Distinguishing these binaries from the $\sim 10^4$ double white dwarfs detectable by LISA will be challenging. In the absence of any other information, the inferred component masses can be used to classify the nature of these objects. However, short-period galactic binaries $\sim 10^7$--$10^3\,\mathrm{yr}$ from coalescence produce a quasi-monochromatic signal which carries little information about their masses. We generate synthetic LISA data sets containing gravitational waves from Galactic binary black holes, binary neutron stars and black hole-neutron stars drawn from an astrophysically realistic population produced through the isolated binary evolution channel. We use a Bayesian inference pipeline to explore the accuracy with which the component masses can be measured. LISA will be able to infer component masses for $\approx 10\% - 50\%$ of the detected systems by measuring the orbital eccentricity, periapse precession frequency, and gravitational-wave induced frequency derivative. Typical fractional mass errors are $\approx 1\%$--$100\%$ (depending on the specific value of the source parameters) enabling the classification of the constituent objects as black holes or neutron stars. For these binaries, LISA will also be able to determine their 3-dimensional position in the Milky Way. LISA detections of these double compact objects will provide new insights to their astrophysical formation processes, the Galactic population, and the Milky Way's star formation history. However, for a significant fraction of the LISA-detected binaries the nature of their constituent objects may remain unclear.

repl.title: Investigating the Gamma-Ray Emission from Explosive Dispersal Outflows with Fermi-LAT
repl.summary: We present the first systematic study of explosive dispersal outflows (EDOs) as potential sources of high-energy emission in the Milky Way. EDOs are energetic outflows produced during dynamical interactions in young, massive star-forming regions, and their physical conditions make them promising environments for cosmic-ray acceleration. Using 16 years of $0.2$--$500$ GeV Fermi-LAT observations, we study the gamma-ray properties of seven EDOs. Three EDOs, DR21, G34.26$+$0.15, and G5.89$-$0.39 show spatially coincident GeV emission, while the remaining systems yield non-detections. Among the sample, DR21 stands out as the brightest candidate, with a detection significance $\geq 40\sigma$. Its spectrum is well described by a power law with an exponential cutoff, and the integrated luminosity in the $0.1$--$500$ GeV band is $L_\gamma \simeq 2\times10^{35}\ \mathrm{erg\ s^{-1}}$. When compared with the outflow's estimated kinetic energy, the inferred cosmic-ray acceleration efficiency is $\leq 15\%$, consistent with values for shocks in dense molecular environments. The energetics and morphology support an association between the DR21 molecular outflow and the observed gamma rays. Our results demonstrate that EDOs span a wide range of gamma-ray luminosities and efficiencies, suggesting they may contribute to the Galactic cosmic ray budget. This motivates searches for additional EDOs and improved multiwavelength characterization of their environments.

repl.title: Hankel low-rank matrix approximation for gravitational-wave data analysis
repl.summary: Next-generation gravitational-wave (GW) detectors, such as the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA), will observe vast numbers of overlapping signals. Disentangling these signals from instrumental noise and from one another constitutes a significant data analysis challenge. We explore a denoising technique based on embedding time series into Hankel matrices: a superposition of $n$ (damped) sinusoids corresponds to a matrix of rank $2n$. Thus, the problem of signal extraction is reduced to a structured low-rank approximation problem. Using synthetic data tailored to GW applications, we benchmark three Hankel-based algorithms: ESPRIT, Cadzow iterations, and iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS). Our test scenarios include isolated and multi-component monochromatic signals, the resolution of sources with closely spaced frequencies, and the recovery of black hole quasinormal modes (QNM). All three algorithms achieve near-optimal performance consistent with Fisher matrix bounds, evidenced by an inverse-square scaling of the mismatch with the signal-to-noise ratio. Furthermore, a proof-of-concept application to numerical relativity waveforms validates the ability of these algorithms to extract QNM frequencies from ringdown signals. Hankel low-rank approximation therefore offers a transparent, computationally efficient avenue for preprocessing GW time series.

repl.title: No Strong Evidence for Plasma Lensing in FRB 20240114A
repl.summary: FRB 20240114A is an extremely active repeating fast radio burst for which plasma lensing has been proposed to explain its burst-rate variations, spectral evolution, and apparently ``carbon-copy'' burst pairs. Using FAST data and publicly available Parkes observations, we test this interpretation with the predictions of a one-dimensional Gaussian plasma-lens model. Although the burst-rate enhancements may be fitted separately for Parkes and FAST, the corresponding magnification peaks and demagnification troughs between the two datasets are offset from each other, inconsistent with plasma lensing predictions. The enhancement peaks also do not show consistent periodicity, disfavoring a binary plasma lensing origin. The burst bandwidths are not systematically narrower during the proposed lensing interval than in other episodes. Most importantly, the burst energy distribution, which shows an intrinsic turnover peak at low energies, shows no significant shift of the turnover during the magnification interval, providing a model-independent test to the plasma-lensing interpretation. All these suggest that there is no strong evidence in favor of a plasma lensing interpretation to the source. Rather, all the burst property variations are consistent with being caused by the intrinsic variations of the FRB central engine.

repl.title: Exploring the connection between Fast Radio Bursts and binary neutron star mergers
repl.summary: Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) are highly energetic radio sources whose duration is of the order of milliseconds. The physical origin of these sources is still unknown. Many models suggest magnetars as possible progenitors of FRBs, and this is supported by the association between FRBs and the Galactic magnetar SGR 1935+2154; other proposed progenitors include binary neutron star (BNS) mergers, that are themselves linked to magnetar formation. In this work we investigate the possible connection between FRBs and BNS mergers, including magnetars that might be produced in such events, by comparing the detection rates inferred from synthetic BNS and associated FRB populations with the rates observed by CHIME. We produce a synthetic catalog of BNS mergers by combining recent theoretically predicted BNS merger rate as a function of redshift and the neutron star mass distribution inferred from measurements of Galactic BNSs. Using this catalog we predict the number of BNS systems ending as magnetars (stable or supramassive neutron star) or black holes (formed promptly or after the collapse of a hypermassive neutron star) for different equations of state. We then simulate for each BNS (and therefore for each magnetar remnant) an associated FRB and estimate how many of them can be potentially detected by CHIME. We find that the rate of BNS mergers and the rate of magnetars produced after BNS represents a non-negligible fraction of the FRBs detected by CHIME, both repeating and non-repeating. Although additional formation channels need to be considered to account for the entire population of FRBs, the existence of a fraction of FRBs that might genuinely be associated to BNS mergers has profound implications in the context of multi- messenger astronomy, supporting the systematic searches of coincident detections of FRBs and GWs from a BNS merger with current and future facilities.

repl.title: Crowdsourcing Gravitational Waves from Superradiant Axions
repl.summary: Black hole superradiance is a powerful probe of ultralight axions. If nature contains a boson with a mass of order $10^{-12}\,$eV, $\textit{mere vacuum fluctuations}$ will lead to its efficient production around spinning stellar mass black holes, forming a gravitational atom that both drains the black hole spin and decays to produce near-monochromatic gravitational waves. Existing superradiance constraints derive primarily from spin measurements of a handful of identified black holes. Here we instead present a detailed study of the population level effect: gravitational waves arising from both the 100 million black holes in the Milky Way and the stochastic signal from axion clouds throughout the universe. We study the impact of a broad range of systematic uncertainties on the black hole properties and compute the projected axion sensitivity for LIGO, as well as the future instruments Einstein Telescope, Cosmic Explorer, and a high-frequency Magnetic Weber Bar. We demonstrate that LIGO can robustly probe axion masses from roughly $10^{-13}\,$eV to $4 \times 10^{-12}\,$eV. If the black hole population extends to masses slightly below $5\,M_{\odot}$ - as hinted for by LIGO inspiral observations - LIGO would approach $10^{-11}\,$eV. Under that same assumption we show that a future high-frequency detector could push considerably higher, potentially beyond $10^{-10}\,$eV in the most optimistic scenarios, reaching towards the lowest masses within the projected sensitivity of axion dark matter searches.

repl.title: Ongoing and Post-Mass-Transfer Binaries: A Living Catalog and Unified Review of Binary Mass Transfer Products
repl.summary: Mass transfer is arguably the most defining interaction in binary stellar systems, yet many aspects of its physics remain poorly understood, from stability to endpoints and observable products. Comparing theory and observations is challenging because post-mass-transfer systems are studied across largely independent communities with different methods, nomenclature, and evolutionary frameworks. % We present a unified review and catalog of ongoing and post-mass-transfer binaries spanning the full stellar mass range, but restricted to systems likely to have experienced only a single episode of mass transfer (i.e., only one component is evolved). We review 16 observational classes of binary interaction products and compile a curated sample of 5,452 systems into a publicly available, community-driven catalog at this https URL . % Using this catalog, we investigate global trends in orbital periods, eccentricities, masses, and mass ratios across post-mass-transfer binaries. We find I) non-zero eccentricities are common at all periods and system classes, with both median values and scatter increasing with period, II) the $e(\log P)$ relation depends on donor progenitor mass, with neutron-star and black-hole binaries showing the highest median eccentricities, likely reflecting effects of natal kicks, III) period distributions are broad and overlapping across evolutionary channels, and IV) the Gaia BH and NS systems are extreme in mass ratio but otherwise consistent with the general post-mass-transfer population. Together, these results support a unified empirical view of post-mass-transfer binaries that highlights several tensions between theory and observations.

repl.title: Linear causality and stability constraints on relativistic second-order magnetohydrodynamics
repl.summary: In this work, we construct a theoretical framework for relativistic second-order magnetohydrodynamics based on entropy current analysis. The formalism consistently incorporates finite relaxation dynamics of the dissipative fluxes, providing a transient framework suitable for analyzing linear stability and short-wavelength causality. Utilizing linear mode analysis, we investigate the constraints imposed by causality and stability on this anisotropic system. By linearizing the theory around a homogeneous equilibrium state, we identify the magnetosonic, Alfvén, and charge-diffusion sectors, together with their coupling terms. For each sector, we derive asymptotic dispersion relations in both the long-wavelength (small-$k$) and short-wavelength (large-$k$) regimes, validating them against exact numerical roots. Our numerical analysis confirms the accuracy of these asymptotic solutions and uncovers a nontrivial angular dependence, especially near special propagation directions where the ordinary momentum expansion becomes less reliable. By evaluating the large-$k$ behavior of the propagating branches alongside the damping properties of non-hydrodynamic modes, we delineate the corresponding causality constraints. We find that the admissible linear causal domain is governed by the interplay between propagation direction, anisotropic transport coefficients, and relaxation times, with the resulting bounds being intrinsically mode-dependent. These findings provide a systematic theoretical basis for investigating linear stability and short-wavelength causality in relativistic magnetohydrodynamics beyond the first-order approximation.

repl.title: Core Composition Effects on the QCD Axion Mass Limit from Neutron Star Cooling
repl.summary: Neutron stars are very dense media in which axions may be produced. This has been used to set a limit on the QCD axion mass, usually under the assumption that only neutrons, protons, electrons, and muons appear in the star core. Given the extreme conditions reached within neutron stars, it is reasonable to consider that other particles, such as hyperons and $\Delta$ resonances, may appear in the neutron star core. In this work, we study how the limit on the mass of QCD axions, namely KSVZ and DFSZ invisible axions, is altered when different equations of state are used, allowing for heavier particles to appear in the neutron star core. We find that this dependence is in general mild and thus reinforces the reliability of the known limit. Additionally, in the DFSZ scenario, it may drive the limit within the sensitivity window for IAXO. This would allow this experiment to discern the composition of neutron star cores if an axion were to be observed within that window.
